argument: Saint Thomas Aquinas fused Aristotle's philosophy with Christian faith, most famously through the unmoved mover argument: since nothing moves without being moved by something else, and this chain cannot regress forever, there must be a first, itself-unmoved mover, which Aquinas calls God. He also resolved the apparent conflict between Aristotle's eternal universe and the Church's creation doctrine by arguing that reason alone cannot prove the world had a beginning, so an eternally existing universe could still be entirely dependent on God as its creator.
keyIdeas: What seems 'obviously' true depends on what alternative explanations an era has available -- ancient Greeks saw cosmic design as obvious before Darwin offered natural selection as an alternative, which matters for reading Aquinas fairly.
In the stick analogy, since a stick only moves when moved by a hand, and that chain of movers cannot regress infinitely, there must be a first, unmoved mover -- which Aquinas identifies as God.
Movement for Aristotle and Aquinas means any change from potentiality to actuality, not just change of location -- wood has the potentiality to become fire, and becoming fire counts as movement.
Aquinas distinguishes the unmoved mover from modern gravity: gravity exists within time and could conceivably have a beginning, while God is eternal and exists external to time altogether.

Aquinas resolved the tension between Aristotle's eternal universe and the Church's creation doctrine by arguing reason alone cannot prove the world had a beginning -- like an eternal foot could produce an eternally existing footprint, an eternal universe could still be entirely dependent on God as its creator.

terms.def: Aristotle's and Aquinas's term for the first cause of all motion, which is itself moved by nothing else.
Aristotle's distinction between what a thing could become (like wood's potential to be fire) and its actual current state; movement is the change from one to the other.
Aquinas's argument, adapted from Aristotle, that the chain of movers in the universe requires a first, unmoved mover, identified as God.

Aquinas's image, quoted in the episode as 'a footprint in the sand is due to the foot that makes it' -- showing something (the universe) can be entirely dependent on its cause (an eternal foot) without that dependence requiring a first moment in time.
Aristotle's view that an infinite physical body is impossible because it couldn't have a coherent 'natural place,' while time can be infinite since every moment has a preceding one.
